 Republicans made Sarah McBride a target. House Democrats just elected her to leadership
 Two years after Republicans targeted her over Capitol bathrooms, Democrats elected the first out transgender member of Congress to help shape their national message.
 Rep. Sarah McBride of Delaware speaks during the second day of the What’s Next post-election Democratic Party gathering on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, at The Mission Ballroom in Denver, Colo. 
 Timothy Hurst/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images
 Christopher Wiggins 
 Nov 20, 2026
 Christopher Wiggins Christopher Wiggins is the politics and news editor at equalpride, where he leads and shapes coverage across The Advocate , Out , and Them . Based in Washington, D.C., he oversees national reporting on the White House, Congress, the Supreme Court, federal agencies, state governments, and the political forces shaping LGBTQ+ life in the United States.
 A GLAAD Media Award-winning journalist, Wiggins has reported extensively on federal policy, civil rights, elections, the courts, and the consequences of government action for LGBTQ+ people, with a particular focus on transgender communities. His work includes cover profiles for The Advocate’s print magazine featuring U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride of Delaware, CNN anchor-turned-independent journalist Don Lemon, former senior Centers for Disease Control and Prevention official Dr. Demetri Daskalakis, and former Vice President Kamala Harris.
 In addition to directing editorial strategy, Wiggins continues to report from Washington on the institutions, officials, and movements defining the national political landscape, including the second Trump administration.
 He can be reached at christopher.wiggins@equalpride.com and followed on Instagram and Bluesky . Whistleblowers and confidential sources may contact him securely on Signal at cwdc.98.

 Follow:
 Christopher Wiggins on X Two years after Republicans tried to make her presence in Congress a national controversy, Sarah McBride has been elected to help lead the Democratic majority taking control of the House in January.
 The Delaware congresswoman, who became the first out transgender person elected to Congress in 2024, made history again Thursday when her colleagues elected her co-chair of the House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee, the caucus’s messaging operation. She is the first trans person elected to a congressional party leadership position.
 McBride received 238 votes, the most among four candidates competing for three co-chair positions, her office confirmed to The Advocate . She will serve alongside Reps. Maxwell Frost of Florida and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California , with Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell chairing the committee.
 The position gives McBride a formal role in shaping how Democrats communicate their priorities, respond to President Donald Trump and make their case to voters ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
 Related : Sarah McBride didn’t give them the fight they wanted. She won anyway 
 “It’s official! I’ve been elected to one of the ten caucus-wide leadership positions for the incoming House Democratic Majority!” McBride wrote Thursday on social media. “I’m so grateful to my colleagues for placing their faith in me to serve as a Democratic Policy and Communications Committee co-chair to help lead our caucus’ messaging in the majority.”
 See on Instagram 
 She outlined the party’s priorities. “Our party stands ready to lower costs, end the war in Iran, combat corruption, and build a government that works for everyone — and we’ll do it by working together,” she wrote.
 Related : Christopher Wiggins wins GLAAD award for Advocate cover story on Sarah McBride
 A strategy built on relationships
 McBride’s election also represents a significant development for a lawmaker who has spent her first term deliberately building relationships with colleagues, including those who disagree with her.
 In a recent interview with The Advocate , McBride reflected on her approach to navigating an institution where personal relationships can matter as much as public confrontations.
 “First and foremost, despite how big the house is as an institution, personal relationships really still matter,” she says.
 “My theory of change has always been about building relationships and trust, and through those relationships and that trust, opening hearts and changing minds and encouraging people to do the right thing,” she says.
 That philosophy has sometimes put McBride at odds with LGBTQ+ supporters who want more confrontational responses to Republican attacks on transgender people. But she argues that political movements need different approaches, including work that rarely goes viral.
 As the only out trans member of Congress, McBride believes she has a particular responsibility to pursue what she calls an “inside strategy,” using relationships and credibility to influence colleagues and legislative outcomes.
 That approach has earned praise from her colleagues. The Democratic Women’s Caucus, where McBride serves as whip, congratulated her Thursday, highlighting her ability to connect with people.
 “Thank you for continuing to use your gift of explaining what’s at stake in a way that connects with people,” the caucus wrote on Facebook. “The DWC is thrilled to see you in this role, and ready to help you get the message out!”
 Related : Sarah McBride opens up about her darkest day in Congress (exclusive)
 From a bathroom ban to a leadership position
 The contrast with McBride’s arrival in Washington is striking.
 In November 2024, shortly after her historic election, Republican Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina, who is leaving Congress in January, introduced a measure targeting transgender women’s access to Capitol bathrooms. House Speaker Mike Johnson, who will pass control of the chamber to Rep. Hakeem Jeffries in January, subsequently imposed restrictions on single-sex facilities under House control.
 McBride opposed the restrictions but said she would comply, arguing that Republicans were trying to distract from issues affecting Americans. Her response drew both praise and criticism within the LGBTQ+ community.
 In her recent interview with The Advocate , McBride revealed the personal toll of those attacks. During a December 2024 photo shoot at the Capitol for an Advocate cover story, she experienced a panic attack.
 “That was my first time back at the Capitol after the bathroom thing,” she says.
 McBride recalled stepping away with a staff member before returning to the photo shoot. The building she had long revered had become a source of distress.
 “That moment in particular is sort of seared into my memory because this place that I had worshiped for so long, revered for so long was the place that was causing me a panic attack,” she says.
 Related : As the first out trans person in Congress, Sarah McBride is ready to fight for us 
 What McBride wants Democrats to do with power
 The Democratic Policy and Communications Committee helps coordinate the party’s policy messaging and public communications. Previous co-chairs include Jeffries, the Democratic nominee for House speaker, and Rep. Ted Lieu of California.
 McBride’s selection places her in discussions about how Democrats communicate on issues Republicans have repeatedly used to divide the party.
 But she has made clear that she wants Democrats to focus on affordability, economic security and government accountability.
 “There has to be accountability, there has to be oversight of this administration,” she told The Advocate , while emphasizing the need to address housing, healthcare and caregiving costs.
 McBride says Jeffries appointed her as a co-convener of the party’s caregiving working group, focused on policies including paid leave, affordable child care and home care.
 “I think the results in Delaware reinforce that my constituents are fair-minded [and that] my constituents are judging candidates based on their ideas and not their identities,” she says.
